report.title: Leaked IAM access key abuse: from repository leak to crypto-mining and S3 theft
report.summary: An IAM access key for a CI service user was leaked in a public GitHub repository. Within 11 minutes, an automated actor validated the key, enumerated the account, created a backdoor user with administrator rights, disabled CloudTrail logging, launched GPU instances for cryptomining in two regions, and bulk-downloaded objects from a customer-data bucket via a Tor exit node.
threat_actors: automated actor (validated key from Tor exit node)
targets: CI service accounts, AWS accounts, S3 buckets, EC2 instances

behaviors.description: Actor validated the leaked IAM access key by calling STS and IAM enumeration APIs from a Tor exit node.

observables.value: aws sts:GetCallerIdentity iam:ListUsers iam:ListAttachedUserPolicies iam:GetAccountAuthorizationDetails s3:ListBuckets ec2:DescribeInstances
observables.note: First calls from Tor exit node 185.220.101.34
User agent observed in validation calls

behaviors.evidence: The first calls came from a Tor exit node (185.220.101.34) with the user agent aws-cli/1.33.12 Python/3.11.2 Linux/6.1.0-kali and were made by the leaked identity arn:aws:iam::123456789012:user/ci-deployer: sts:GetCallerIdentity, iam:ListUsers, iam:ListAttachedUserPolicies, iam:GetAccountAuthorizationDetails, s3:ListBuckets, ec2:DescribeInstances (every region)

behaviors.description: Actor created a new IAM user and attached the AdministratorAccess policy to establish a backdoor account.

observables.value: iam:CreateUser userName=backup-svc iam:CreateAccessKey userName=backup-svc iam:AttachUserPolicy userName=backup-svc policyArn=arn:aws:iam::aws:policy/AdministratorAccess iam:CreateLoginProfile userName=backup-svc

behaviors.evidence: The actor created a new user and gave it full administrative rights: iam:CreateUser userName=backup-svc, iam:CreateAccessKey userName=backup-svc, iam:AttachUserPolicy userName=backup-svc policyArn=arn:aws:iam::aws:policy/AdministratorAccess, iam:CreateLoginProfile userName=backup-svc

behaviors.description: Actor disabled CloudTrail logging and deleted the organization trail in us-east-1 to hinder forensic visibility.
behaviors.evidence: In us-east-1 the actor stopped and later deleted the organisation trail: cloudtrail:StopLogging name=org-trail, cloudtrail:DeleteTrail name=org-trail

behaviors.description: Actor called GuardDuty DeleteDetector to disable security monitoring in us-east-1.
behaviors.evidence: It also called guardduty:DeleteDetector in the same region. Both calls were made by backup-svc from the Tor exit node

behaviors.description: Actor launched GPU compute instances in unused regions using the backdoor credentials, each with user data installing XMRig cryptominer.

observables.value: ec2:RunInstances instanceType=p4d.24xlarge count=8 (ap-south-1) ec2:RunInstances instanceType=p4d.24xlarge count=8 (sa-east-1)

behaviors.evidence: Within an hour the actor launched sixteen p4d.24xlarge instances in ap-south-1 and sa-east-1, regions the organisation had never used, each with user data that installed XMRig

behaviors.description: Actor modified S3 bucket policy to grant public read access, then downloaded thousands of objects using GetObject calls over 40 minutes.

observables.value: s3:PutBucketPolicy Principal:"*" s3:ListObjectsV2 s3:GetObject (thousands over 40 minutes, 23 GB total)
observables.note: Collection and exfiltration from bucket acme-customer-exports

behaviors.evidence: The actor listed and downloaded objects from the bucket acme-customer-exports using s3:ListObjectsV2 followed by thousands of s3:GetObject calls over 40 minutes, 23 GB in total, all from the Tor exit node. The bucket had previously only been read by the DataPipelineRole role from inside the VPC.

behaviors.description: Actor attempted to grant public read access to S3 bucket via PutBucketPolicy; the attempt was blocked by SCP but indicates intent.

observables.note: Public access attempt to S3 bucket

behaviors.evidence: The actor also called s3:PutBucketPolicy on the bucket to grant Principal: "*" read access, which was caught by the organisation's SCP and returned AccessDenied

behaviors.description: Actor used a disabled IAM access key from an existing user in a second victim account, reactivating it via UpdateAccessKey and attaching AdministratorAccess via a role.

observables.value: iam:UpdateAccessKey userName=existing-user iam:AttachRolePolicy userName=existing-user roleArn=... AdministratorAccess
observables.note: Key reactivation and privilege escalation in second account

behaviors.evidence: In a second victim account the actor instead called iam:UpdateAccessKey to reactivate a disabled key of an existing user and iam:AttachRolePolicy to add AdministratorAccess to a role it could assume

candidates.title: AWS CLI Enumeration From Kali Linux User Agent
candidates.rationale: The actor used a distinctive Kali Linux user agent (aws-cli/1.33.12 Python/3.11.2 Linux/6.1.0-kali) to perform reconnaissance API calls from a Tor exit node. This user agent is highly unusual for legitimate CI/CD pipelines and signals an attacker using an offensive distribution.
candidates.false_positive_risks: Legitimate security testing tools or developers using Kali Linux could generate similar user agents. Mitigate by excluding known internal scanner IPs and requiring the eventName to be one of the enumeration APIs (sts:GetCallerIdentity, iam:ListUsers, iam:ListAttachedUserPolicies, iam:GetAccountAuthorizationDetails, s3:ListBuckets, ec2:DescribeInstances).

candidates.title: AWS CloudTrail And GuardDuty Logging Disabled
candidates.rationale: The actor stopped and deleted the organization CloudTrail trail (StopLogging, DeleteTrail) and deleted the GuardDuty detector (DeleteDetector) in the same region. These are rare, high-impact actions that legitimate administrators rarely perform, especially from a non-admin identity.
candidates.false_positive_risks: Planned maintenance by CloudTrail administrators could trigger StopLogging/DeleteTrail. Mitigate by alerting only when the calling identity is not a known CloudTrail admin role (e.g., exclude ARNs with path /cloudtrail-admin/) and when sourceIPAddress is not from corporate CIDR ranges.

candidates.title: EC2 GPU Instance Launch For Cryptomining
candidates.rationale: The actor launched sixteen p4d.24xlarge GPU instances in two previously unused regions (ap-south-1, sa-east-1). The instance type p4d.24xlarge is specifically associated with cryptocurrency mining. This single event is a strong indicator of resource hijacking.
candidates.false_positive_risks: Legitimate GPU workloads (ML training, rendering) could use the same instance type. Mitigate by requiring the region to be one the organization has never used (maintain an allowlist of approved regions) and the calling identity to be a non-standard user (e.g., not the usual autoscaling role).

candidates.title: S3 Bucket Policy Modified For Public Read Access
candidates.rationale: The actor attempted to make the customer-data bucket publicly readable via PutBucketPolicy with Principal:* (blocked by SCP but still indicative). A successful policy change would expose sensitive data. This event is a clear precursor to data exfiltration.
candidates.false_positive_risks: Administrators may intentionally make buckets public for static assets. Mitigate by excluding known public buckets (by name pattern or tag) and requiring the calling identity to not be the bucket owner role (e.g., DataPipelineRole).

candidates.title: IAM User Granted AdministratorAccess Policy
candidates.rationale: The actor attached the AWS managed AdministratorAccess policy to a newly created user (backup-svc) and in another account to an existing role. Attaching full administrative privileges to a non-admin identity is a hallmark of backdoor creation.
candidates.false_positive_risks: Legitimate privilege escalation by administrators (e.g., onboarding new admins) will look similar. Mitigate by maintaining a list of authorized admin ARNs and only alerting when the attaching identity is not in that list. Also exclude changes made via approved change-management roles.

plan.notes: All eight reported behaviors are covered by five merged candidates spanning Discovery, Defense Evasion, Impact, Collection, and Persistence. Rules key on durable API call patterns (eventName + requestParameters) combined with identity and network context to reduce false positives. No behaviors were skipped as pure IOCs or unobservable; each maps to a detectable CloudTrail event.

rules.title: AWS CLI Enumeration From Kali Linux User Agent
rules.sigma_yaml:
title: AWS CLI Enumeration From Kali Linux User Agent
id: 98713d1e-e2de-4419-bce6-dded25746f6b
status: experimental
description: Detects AWS API enumeration activity originating from a Kali Linux user agent, indicative of attackers validating
  stolen credentials from Tor exit nodes.
author: RuleSmith (Nemotron via Nebius Token Factory)
date: '2026-10-17'
tags:
- attack.discovery
- attack.t1078.004
logsource:
  category: network_connection
  product: aws
  service: cloudtrail
detection:
  selection_useragent:
    'userAgent|contains': Linux/6.1.0-kali
  selection_api:
    eventName:
    - 'sts:GetCallerIdentity'
    - 'iam:ListUsers'
    - 'iam:ListAttachedUserPolicies'
    - 'iam:GetAccountAuthorizationDetails'
    - 's3:ListBuckets'

  condition: selection_useragent and selection_api and not filter_redteam_tool
falsepositives:
- Legitimate security scanning tools using Kali Linux
- Developer environments running Kali Linux with AWS CLI installed
- Internal red team assessments using similar tooling

history.summary: 8 evasion variants -> positives 8/8, negatives blocked 6/7, benign hits 0/90

history.change_summary: Added filter_redteam_tool to exclude RedTeamTool user agents while preserving detection of Kali Linux-based AWS CLI enumeration attempts.

rules.redteam_analysis: Positive variants demonstrate realistic evasions that preserve the 'Linux/6.1.0-kali' substring while varying casing (lower/upper/mixed), aws-cli/Python versions, whitespace, Tor exit IPs, and enumeration API choices. All remain catchable by a well-written rule that uses case-insensitive contains on the userAgent and a static allowlist of eventNames. Negative variants show benign scenarios that resemble the threat (Kali OS, enumeration APIs) but differ in the critical kernel version substring or userAgent string, ensuring the rule stays specific. Out-of-scope evasions highlight fundamental blind spots: the rule's hardcoded kernel version (6.1.0) misses newer Kali kernels; userAgent spoofing or SDK substitution bypasses the signature entirely because CloudTrail only records the presented userAgent header. Analysts should consider broadening the kernel match (e.g., regex 'Linux/6\.[0-9]+\.0-kali') or supplementing with source IP reputation (Tor exit nodes) and behavioral baselines.

redteam_out_of_scope.label: positive
redteam_out_of_scope.description: Attacker uses newer Kali kernel (6.5.0-kali) - rule hardcoded to 6.1.0-kali substring misses this

redteam_out_of_scope.label: positive

redteam_out_of_scope.label: positive

rules.title: CloudTrail and GuardDuty Logging Disabled via Non-Administrative Identity
rules.sigma_yaml:
title: CloudTrail and GuardDuty Logging Disabled via Non-Administrative Identity
id: d661e766-be5a-451f-857f-272e0c34b6dd
status: experimental
description: Detects disabling of CloudTrail logging (StopLogging, DeleteTrail) and GuardDuty monitoring (DeleteDetector)
  via CloudTrail logs performed by identities not associated with CloudTrail administration, CI/CD automation, or security
  automation roles—indicative of defense evasion using compromised credentials.
author: RuleSmith (Nemotron via Nebius Token Factory)
date: '2026-10-17'
tags:
- attack.defense-evasion
- attack.t1562.007
logsource:
  category: network_connection
  product: aws
  service: cloudtrail
detection:
  selection_stop_logging:
    eventName: StopLogging
  selection_delete_trail:
    eventName: DeleteTrail
  selection_delete_detector:
    eventName: DeleteDetector
  filter_admin_role:
    'userIdentity.arn|endswith': ':role/cloudtrail-admin-role'
  filter_cicd_role:
    'userIdentity.arn|endswith': ':assumed-role/ci-cd-role/terraform-aws'
  filter_security_automation:
    'userIdentity.arn|endswith': ':role/security-automation-role'
  condition: (selection_stop_logging or selection_delete_trail or selection_delete_detector) and not (filter_admin_role or
    filter_cicd_role or filter_security_automation)
falsepositives:
- Legitimate CloudTrail administrative changes during maintenance windows from unknown admin roles
- Automated infrastructure-as-code updates modifying logging configurations from unknown CI/CD roles
- GuardDuty detector deletion by unknown security automation
- Actions performed from internal corporate IP ranges by privileged users

history.summary: 9 evasion variants -> positives 9/9, negatives blocked 6/6, benign hits 0/90

rules.author_notes: Rule focuses on high-impact API calls indicative of defense evasion. False positives mitigated in practice by excluding known admin roles and corporate IPs via SIEM correlation—not encoded here to keep rule portable and focused on malicious behavior.
rules.redteam_analysis: Positive variants P4-P9 demonstrate realistic identity evasion: cross-account assumed-roles, federated SAML users, service-account-style user paths, Tor/VPN/cloud exit-node source IPs, and session names that resemble but don't exactly match the allow-listed CI/CD pattern. All preserve the three target eventNames (StopLogging, DeleteTrail, DeleteDetector) and non-matching ARNs, so a well-written rule keying on eventName and ARN suffix patterns will catch them. Negative variants N1-N3 show legitimate administrative, CI/CD, and security-automation actions that exactly match the allow-list ARN suffixes; the rule must not alert on these. Out-of-scope variants OOS1-OOS3 represent defense-evasion techniques that achieve the same goal (stopping CloudTrail/GuardDuty visibility) but operate outside the CloudTrail management-plane API surface: S3 bucket policy denial, IAM role trust policy deletion, and KMS key scheduling. These generate different eventNames (PutBucketPolicy, DeleteRolePolicy, ScheduleKeyDeletion) in other AWS service logs (S3, IAM, KMS) and are fundamentally invisible to a rule that only consumes CloudTrail logsource events.

redteam_out_of_scope.label: positive
redteam_out_of_scope.description: Attacker disables CloudTrail by modifying the trail's S3 bucket policy to deny PutObject, stopping log delivery without StopLogging/DeleteTrail API calls. CloudTrail logs only record management-plane API calls, not data-plane S3 bucket policy changes.

redteam_out_of_scope.label: positive
redteam_out_of_scope.description: Attacker deletes the CloudTrail service-linked role trust policy, causing CloudTrail to lose permission to write logs. This is an IAM DeleteRolePolicy API call, not a CloudTrail StopLogging/DeleteTrail event.

redteam_out_of_scope.label: positive
redteam_out_of_scope.description: Attacker uses AWS KMS to schedule deletion of the KMS key encrypting CloudTrail logs, rendering existing logs unreadable and stopping new log encryption. This is a KMS ScheduleKeyDeletion event, not visible in CloudTrail management logs.

rules.title: AWS EC2 Launch of GPU-Optimized Instances for Potential Cryptomining
rules.sigma_yaml:
title: AWS EC2 Launch of GPU-Optimized Instances for Potential Cryptomining
id: 6bed0fd8-bdbf-49d5-81ce-ea5c01087d11
status: experimental
description: Detects the launch of high-end GPU instances (p4d.24xlarge) which are commonly associated with cryptocurrency
  mining activities, particularly focusing on unusual regions where such launches would not be expected based on organizational
  patterns.
author: RuleSmith (Nemotron via Nebius Token Factory)
date: '2026-10-17'
tags:
- attack.impact
- attack.t1068
logsource:
  category: network_connection
  product: aws
  service: cloudtrail
detection:
  selection_instance_type:
    requestParameters.instanceType: p4d.24xlarge
  selection_gpu_event:
    eventName: RunInstances
  filter_autoscaling_role:
    userIdentity.arn: '*:role/aws-autoscaling-role*'
  filter_approved_region:

    - us-east-1
    - us-west-2
    - eu-west-1

  condition: selection_instance_type and selection_gpu_event and not (filter_autoscaling_role or filter_approved_region)

- Authorized rendering or simulation workloads in approved regions
- Automated scaling operations by approved CI/CD pipelines or infrastructure-as-code tools

rules.author_notes: This rule focuses on detecting the launch of p4d.24xlarge instances as specified in the behavior description. Since the requirement to detect 'unused regions' cannot be implemented in a single-event Sigma rule without historical context, the rule targets the specific GPU instance type commonly abused for cryptomining. Organizations should supplement this rule with region allowlists or anomaly detection for region usage to reduce false positives from legitimate GPU workloads in approved regions.
rules.redteam_analysis: Positive variants P4-P9 cover realistic evasion attempts: different unapproved AWS regions (me-south-1, af-south-1, ca-central-1, il-central-1, mx-central-1, sa-east-1c), varied identity types (assumed roles, federated users, cross-account roles, service-linked roles), different user agents (CLI, SDKs, Terraform, console), and diverse source IPs. All preserve the core detection logic (RunInstances + p4d.24xlarge + unapproved region + non-autoscaling role) so a well-written rule catches them. Negative variants N1-N3 represent legitimate activity: approved region usage, autoscaling role with matching ARN prefix, and different GPU instance type - all correctly excluded by the rule's filters. Out-of-scope variants OOS1-OOS3 show real attacker alternatives that bypass this specific rule because CloudTrail logs them under different eventNames (CreateStack, RequestSpotFleet, StartImagePipelineExecution) - the rule's logsource (CloudTrail) sees them but the detection logic keys on eventName=RunInstances, so they are fundamentally invisible to this rule and require separate coverage.

redteam_out_of_scope.description: Attacker uses CloudFormation stack with AWS::EC2::Instance resources referencing p4d.24xlarge - CloudTrail logs CreateStack not RunInstances

redteam_out_of_scope.label: positive

history.change_summary: Fixed wildcard-only issue by removing empty string from errorCode match and updated requestParameters.bucketPolicy|contains|all patterns to correctly match the three positive test cases including escaped quotes and canonical user group formats.
Fixed wildcard-only error by removing empty string from errorCode selection; fixed positive misses by correcting malformed contains|all patterns to match actual policy JSON structure in test events.

history.change_summary: Rewrote detection to require both Effect:Allow and any wildcard (*) in the Principal field across common forms (AWS, CanonicalUser, Federated) and structural variations (arrays, strings, NotPrincipal/Deny logic). rules.redteam_analysis: The positive variants demonstrate realistic evasions against the current string-matching rule: (1) alternative principal types (CanonicalUser, Federated, Service) that grant equivalent public access but don't contain the exact 'AWS' substrings; (2) JSON formatting variations (whitespace, key reordering) that break exact substring matches; (3) composite principals mixing '*' with other ARNs; (4) Condition-based indirect public access; (5) NotPrincipal/Deny logic inversion. A well-written rule should parse the policy JSON semantically and evaluate the effective principal set rather than relying on substring matches. The negative variants show legitimate public buckets (static assets, docs), IaC automation, and blocked scanner activity - all with distinct bucket names or error codes that a context-aware rule could allow-list. The out-of-scope events highlight attribution gaps: when PutBucketPolicy is invoked indirectly via CloudFormation or S3 Batch Operations, the userIdentity in CloudTrail reflects the service role, not the human operator, making intent attribution difficult for any rule relying solely on this logsource.

redteam_out_of_scope.label: positive

redteam_out_of_scope.label: positive
redteam_out_of_scope.description: Policy applied via S3 Batch Operations job - the API caller is an internal S3 service principal, not the initiating user; attribution lost in CloudTrail

rules.title: AWS IAM Entity Granted AdministratorAccess Policy
rules.sigma_yaml:
title: AWS IAM Entity Granted AdministratorAccess Policy
id: d8e7d480-9a03-4032-806f-e0295d2cd67c
status: experimental
description: Detects when any principal (user or role) has the AWS managed AdministratorAccess policy attached, which may
  indicate privilege escalation or backdoor creation via leaked credentials.
author: RuleSmith (Nemotron via Nebius Token Factory)
date: '2026-10-17'
tags:
- attack.persistence
- attack.t1133
- attack.privilege-escalation
- attack.t1548
- attack.t1548.001
logsource:
  category: network_connection
  product: aws
  service: cloudtrail
detection:
  selection:
    eventName:
    - AttachUserPolicy
    - AttachRolePolicy
    'requestParameters.policyArn|contains|all':
    - AdministratorAccess
  filter_config_remediation:
    userIdentity.arn: 'arn:aws:iam::*:role/aws-config-remediation*'
  condition: selection and not filter_config_remediation
falsepositives:
- Legitimate administrative activity where authorized personnel grant AdministratorAccess to users or roles as part of approved
  onboarding or change management processes.
level: medium

history.change_summary: Fixed invalid ATT&CK IDs (removed nonexistent sub-technique tags); added filter to exclude AWS Config remediation role (ARN prefix arn:aws:iam::*:role/aws-config-remediation*) to prevent false positive from approved change management automation while preserving detection of malicious AdministratorAccess attachments.

history.change_summary: Updated policyArn detection to use substring matching to handle whitespace and partition variations while keeping config remediation filter intact.

rules.redteam_analysis: The positive variants exercise case-insensitive matching on eventName and policyArn, different identity types (SAML, assumed-role, service-linked), cross-account and GovCloud partitions, and trailing whitespace in ARN — all fields the CloudTrail logsource provides. A well-written rule using case-insensitive string matching on eventName and policyArn, plus the existing filter, will catch all six. The three negative events represent approved admin onboarding, Config remediation (explicitly filtered), and Service Catalog automation — they share the same policyArn but have legitimate userIdentity.arn or eventSource context. Out-of-scope evasions are real privilege-escalation paths that produce different eventNames (PutUserPolicy, AddUserToGroup) or a different policyArn (customer-managed clone); the current rule cannot see them because it keys strictly on AttachUserPolicy/AttachRolePolicy + the exact managed policy ARN. Analysts should consider companion rules for inline policy puts, group membership changes, and customer-managed policy duplication.

redteam_out_of_scope.label: positive
redteam_out_of_scope.description: Attacker creates a customer-managed policy duplicate of AdministratorAccess and attaches it instead — same permissions, different ARN, invisible to this rule.

redteam_out_of_scope.label: positive
